title: CBD and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Mix? Sedation, Liver, and CBD Drinks
excerpt: Can you mix CBD and alcohol? How hemp CBD and drinking add up in your brain and liver, medication interactions, CBD drinks, hangovers, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Is it safe to mix CBD and alcohol? How hemp CBD adds to alcohol's sedation, liver and medication risks, CBD drinks, hangovers, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** for most healthy adults, a typical dose of hemp-derived CBD and a drink or two is unlikely to cause a serious problem, but the two do add to each other. Both can make you drowsy and slow your reactions, and in the small amount of human research that exists, people who took CBD with alcohol were more impaired on coordination tests than with alcohol alone. Both are also processed by your liver, and high-dose CBD can raise liver enzymes on its own. The combination gets riskier with bigger doses of either, with daily drinking, and with prescription medicines that also cause drowsiness or depend on the liver.

**The quick rules:** Treat CBD like a mild sedative when you drink. Keep both doses modest, don't use CBD to "take the edge off" a night of heavy drinking, and never drive after mixing them. If you take prescription medicine (especially for seizures, anxiety, sleep, pain, depression, or blood clotting), have liver disease, or drink most days, talk to your doctor or pharmacist before using CBD at all. And check the label: if a product contains THC, the advice in this article doesn't cover it, and the combination is noticeably stronger.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and safety guidance about hemp-derived CBD. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor before using CBD if** you take any prescription medicine, you have liver disease or have been told your liver enzymes are high, you drink alcohol most days, or you're pregnant or breastfeeding. **Get medical help right away if** someone who mixed CBD (or any cannabis product) with alcohol is very hard to wake, breathing slowly, vomiting while drowsy, or confused. In an emergency, call 911.

## What CBD Actually Is (and What It Isn't)

CBD stands for **cannabidiol**. It's one of more than a hundred compounds found in the cannabis plant. The other famous one is THC (tetrahydrocannabinol), the compound that makes people feel high. CBD doesn't produce a high in the usual sense, though it can make some people feel calm, relaxed, or sleepy.

Most CBD sold in shops, gas stations, and online in the US comes from **hemp**, which is cannabis grown to contain very little THC. Under the 2018 Farm Bill, hemp is defined as cannabis with no more than 0.3% delta-9 THC by dry weight. That's why CBD products are so widely available. Hemp rules have been tightening since then, and what's legal varies a lot by state, so it's worth checking where you live.

CBD comes in a lot of forms:

- **Oils and tinctures** that you drop under your tongue
- **Gummies and capsules**
- **Vapes and smokable hemp flower**
- **Topicals** such as creams and balms
- **CBD drinks**, including sparkling waters, "social tonics," and CBD-infused mocktails sold as alcohol alternatives

There are also three broad types of CBD extract you'll see on labels:

- **Isolate:** pure CBD with the other plant compounds removed. Should contain no THC.
- **Broad-spectrum:** many plant compounds, with the THC removed (or reduced to very low levels).
- **Full-spectrum:** many plant compounds, including small amounts of THC (legally up to 0.3% by dry weight in hemp). In a large dose, that small percentage can add up.

There's one FDA-approved CBD medicine in the US, **Epidiolex**, a prescription oral solution used for certain rare seizure disorders. Much of what we know about CBD's side effects comes from its clinical trials, which used doses far higher than what's in a typical gummy. Everything else on the shelf is unapproved, and the FDA has said that CBD can't legally be added to food or sold as a dietary supplement, although enforcement has been limited. In practice, that means CBD products aren't checked for what's in them before they're sold.

This article is about hemp-derived CBD. **THC products are a different story**, and we cover them briefly below.

## How CBD and Alcohol Interact: The Brain Side

Alcohol is a depressant. It boosts the brain's main calming signal (a chemical messenger called GABA) and dampens its main excitatory one, which is why a few drinks relax you and too many make you clumsy, slurred, and sleepy. Our [GABA guide](/never-hungover/gaba-gamma-aminobutyric-acid-complete-guide-benefits-dosage-natural-sources-2025) explains that chemistry in more detail.

CBD works differently. It doesn't plug into the brain's cannabinoid receptors the way THC does. Instead, it nudges several systems at once, including serotonin receptors, the body's own cannabinoid signaling, and, according to lab research, the GABA system. The overall effect, especially at higher doses, can be calming and sedating.

Drowsiness is one of the most consistent side effects of CBD. In the clinical trials behind Epidiolex, sleepiness and sedation were among the most common side effects, and the prescribing information warns that combining it with other substances that slow the brain, **including alcohol**, may increase that sedation. Lower retail doses produce less sleepiness, but the direction is the same.

So when you combine CBD and alcohol, you're stacking two things that can both make you drowsy and slow your reactions. For most people at modest doses the extra effect is small. For some people, especially those who are light, new to CBD, tired, or taking a large dose, it can be very noticeable.

### What the human research shows

The research on mixing CBD and alcohol in people is thin. The best-known study is old and small: in 1979, researchers gave 10 healthy volunteers CBD, alcohol, both, or a placebo and tested their coordination and reaction times. The alcohol plus CBD combination produced significant impairment in motor and psychomotor performance compared with placebo. Oddly, blood alcohol levels were lower when CBD was added, but people were still impaired, so a lower reading did not mean they were safer.

Ten people in one lab session is not enough to draw firm conclusions, and no large modern trial has settled the question. What we can say plainly is this: **there is no good evidence that CBD makes alcohol safer, and some evidence that the two add up.**

### What this means on a night out

- If you've taken CBD, expect each drink to hit a bit harder than usual, especially the first time you combine them.
- Don't drive, cycle, or operate anything risky after mixing them, even if you "feel fine." Sedation can creep up, and your judgment about your own impairment is one of the first things alcohol dulls.
- Start low with both if you're going to mix them at all: a small CBD dose and fewer drinks than usual.

## How CBD and Alcohol Interact: The Liver Side

Your liver does most of the work of breaking down both alcohol and CBD, but they mostly use different routes.

**Alcohol** is broken down mainly by an enzyme called alcohol dehydrogenase, which turns it into acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product. A second enzyme then turns acetaldehyde into harmless acetate. Heavy, regular drinking also switches on a backup enzyme system that changes how the liver handles many drugs.

**CBD** is processed by the liver's drug-handling enzymes, a family called cytochrome P450 (mainly the ones labeled CYP3A4 and CYP2C19). CBD can also slow those same enzymes down, which is why it can raise the blood levels of some medicines. That's the main reason pharmacists care about CBD.

There's also a direct liver signal. In the Epidiolex trials, some patients developed raised liver enzymes (a blood test sign that the liver is under stress). This was more common at higher doses and in people also taking another seizure drug, valproate, and it usually reversed when the dose was lowered or stopped. Smaller studies in healthy adults taking high daily doses of CBD have also found that a minority develop raised liver enzymes. The FDA has listed possible liver injury among its concerns about unregulated CBD.

What does that mean for an ordinary drinker? For a healthy person taking a modest CBD dose and drinking moderately, the liver risk from the combination is probably low. But the risk climbs when you add more of each:

- **Heavy or daily drinking** already strains the liver.
- **High-dose CBD** (hundreds of milligrams a day) can raise liver enzymes on its own.
- **Other medicines processed by the liver** add another layer.

If you're in any of those groups, it's worth asking your doctor to check your liver enzymes if you plan to use CBD regularly.

### Does CBD protect your liver from alcohol?

You'll see this claim in CBD marketing. It comes from rodent studies in which CBD reduced some signs of alcohol-related liver damage, such as fat build-up and inflammation. Those results are interesting, but animal results often don't carry over to people, and the doses used aren't comparable to a gummy. **There is no good evidence that CBD protects the human liver from alcohol.** Don't use it as a reason to drink more.

## CBD, Alcohol, and Medications

This is where the real risks are. CBD's effect on liver enzymes means it can change how other drugs behave, and alcohol carries its own warnings with many of the same medicines. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before using CBD if you take any of the following, and especially before adding alcohol on top:

- **Seizure medicines**, such as clobazam and valproate. CBD can raise clobazam levels (more sedation), and combining CBD with valproate is linked to liver enzyme rises.
- **Blood thinners**, especially warfarin. CBD can raise warfarin levels and increase bleeding risk, and alcohol affects warfarin too. Our guide to [blood thinners and alcohol](/never-hungover/blood-thinners-and-alcohol) explains that side of it.
- **Benzodiazepines and sleep medicines**, such as Xanax, Valium, Ativan, or zolpidem. These already carry serious warnings about alcohol. Adding CBD piles on more sedation. See our article on [Xanax and alcohol](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol) for why that combination is dangerous.
- **Opioid pain medicines.** Opioids plus alcohol can slow breathing, and adding another sedative makes that worse.
- **Antidepressants and anti-anxiety medicines**, including SSRIs. Some are processed by the same liver enzymes CBD affects, and most carry alcohol warnings of their own.
- **Nerve-pain medicines** such as gabapentin and pregabalin, which add sedation. Our [gabapentin and alcohol](/never-hungover/gabapentin-and-alcohol) article covers that interaction.
- **Antihistamines that cause drowsiness**, such as diphenhydramine (Benadryl) and doxylamine (Unisom).
- **Any medicine with a "grapefruit warning"** on the label. Grapefruit affects the same liver enzyme (CYP3A4) that CBD does, so that warning is a useful red flag that CBD may interact too.

This list isn't complete. If you take any prescription medicine, the safest move is a quick conversation with a pharmacist, who can check your full list. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers how common supplements and medicines interact more broadly.

## CBD Drinks: Are They a Good Alternative to Alcohol?

CBD drinks are marketed as a way to relax socially without alcohol, and for some people they do that job. If you're cutting back, replacing a second or third drink with a CBD seltzer can make a night feel less like abstinence. There are honest pros and cons.

**Pros:**

- No alcohol, so no hangover from the drink itself, no alcohol calories, and no acetaldehyde for your liver to process.
- Hemp CBD at typical doses doesn't cause a high or lead to the kind of impairment alcohol does.
- Something to hold and sip, which is half the point of a social drink for many people.

**Cons:**

- **Dose and content are uncertain.** CBD isn't evaluated before sale, and independent testing has repeatedly found products that don't match their labels. A 2017 study in *JAMA* that tested CBD products bought online found only about a third were accurately labeled; many had more or less CBD than claimed, and some contained THC.
- **Many drinks contain very little CBD**, and CBD in water-based drinks may be poorly absorbed, so some do little beyond what a plain sparkling water would.
- **Some "hemp drinks" contain THC.** A growing number of hemp-derived beverages contain enough THC to make you high. Read the label carefully; a "hemp" or "cannabis" drink is not automatically a CBD-only drink.
- **They don't mix well with alcohol.** A CBD drink is a good swap for a drink, not a mixer for one. CBD cocktails combine the two, with the sedation effects described above.

**The bottom line on CBD drinks:** used *instead of* alcohol, a CBD-only drink from a brand that publishes third-party test results is a reasonable option for most healthy adults. Used *with* alcohol, it adds risk without adding much benefit.

## Can You Take CBD After Drinking? (CBD for a Hangover)

This is one of the most common questions, and the honest answer is that **there is no good evidence that CBD helps with a hangover.** No controlled trial has tested it.

Some of the marketing claims are based on reasonable-sounding ideas: CBD may ease anxiety in some studies, cannabis compounds can affect nausea, and some lab work suggests anti-inflammatory effects. But most of the evidence for nausea relief involves THC, not CBD, and a hangover is mainly driven by things CBD doesn't touch, such as poor sleep, dehydration, low blood sugar, acetaldehyde, and the inflammation that follows heavy drinking.

If you do take CBD the morning after:

- **Wait until the alcohol has fully cleared.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies a lot. If you drank late and heavily, there may still be alcohol in your system in the morning.
- **Keep the dose modest** and don't drive until you know how it affects you.
- **Don't use it as a sleep aid right after drinking.** If you can't sleep after a night out, adding a sedative on top of alcohol isn't a great idea. Our article on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains what's going on and safer ways to handle it.

### "Hangxiety" and CBD

Morning-after anxiety ("hangxiety") is real, and it's partly the brain rebounding after alcohol's calming effect wears off. Some small studies suggest CBD may reduce anxiety in certain situations, such as a public-speaking test, but the results are mixed and none tested hangovers. If anxiety after drinking is a regular pattern for you, our guide to [alcohol and anxiety](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-anxiety-breaking-the-cycle-naturally-2025) covers why it happens and what actually helps. Drinking less in the first place is the most reliable fix.

## Can You Drink Alcohol After Taking CBD?

There's no official waiting time. CBD's effects from an oil or gummy typically build over the first one to two hours and fade over several hours, but how long they last depends on the dose, the form, whether you ate, and your body. The compound itself stays in your body much longer than the feeling, especially with daily use.

Some sensible guidance:

- **Occasional low dose (say a 10 to 25 mg gummy) and a drink or two:** likely fine for most healthy adults not on interacting medicines, but expect the drinks to feel a little stronger and don't drive.
- **Larger dose or new product:** wait until you know how that product affects you on its own before adding alcohol.
- **Daily CBD user:** CBD builds up in the body with regular use, so "waiting a few hours" doesn't really clear it. Keep drinking light and talk to your doctor if you're on other medicines.

## Does CBD Help With Cutting Back on Drinking?

You may have seen headlines about CBD and alcohol cravings. They're mostly based on animal studies, in which CBD reduced alcohol intake and relapse-like behavior in rodents, plus early, small human studies. It's an active research area, but **there is no good evidence yet that CBD reliably helps people drink less**, and it's not an approved treatment for anything alcohol-related.

That said, if swapping a nightly beer for a CBD seltzer helps you build a new routine, that's a perfectly reasonable experiment for most healthy adults. The drink you didn't have is what does the good work.

One important note: if you've been drinking heavily every day and you get shaky, sweaty, anxious, or have a racing heart when you stop, that can be alcohol withdrawal. It can become dangerous and there are effective medical treatments for it, so talk to a doctor rather than trying to manage it with CBD or any other supplement.

## What About THC, Delta-8, and "Crossfading"?

Many products sold near CBD contain THC: dispensary cannabis, delta-9 THC edibles and drinks made from hemp, and delta-8 THC products. Mixing those with alcohol ("crossfading") is a very different situation from mixing alcohol with CBD.

- **The impairment is much stronger.** THC affects coordination, reaction time, and judgment on its own, and combining it with alcohol makes driving impairment worse than either alone.
- **Nausea and "the spins" are common**, especially when people drink first and then use cannabis.
- **Edibles and drinks are slow**, so it's easy to take more before the first dose kicks in, then have both peak together.
- **Some research suggests alcohol can raise THC levels in the blood** when the two are used together.

If you're comparing the two substances more broadly, our article on [cannabis vs alcohol](/never-hungover/cannabis-vs-alcohol-complete-health-comparison-for-wellness-minded-adults) goes through the health differences in detail.

## Drug Tests and CBD

A practical warning that catches people out: **CBD products can make you fail a drug test.** Standard workplace drug tests look for THC, not CBD. But full-spectrum products contain some THC by design, and mislabeled "THC-free" products sometimes do too. Daily use of a high-dose full-spectrum product can add up. If you're tested at work, choose a product with a recent third-party certificate of analysis showing no detectable THC, and know that even then there's some risk. Alcohol itself, of course, can show up on breath and some urine tests.

## How CBD Compares With Other Calming Supplements and Alcohol

People often reach for CBD alongside other "relaxing" supplements. The common theme is that most of them add sedation when combined with alcohol:

- **Kava** is a stronger concern, with both added sedation and rare liver injury. See our guide to [kava and alcohol](/never-hungover/kava-and-alcohol).
- **Ashwagandha** has its own sedation and liver questions. See [ashwagandha and alcohol](/never-hungover/ashwagandha-and-alcohol).
- **Melatonin** is a sleep signal rather than a sedative, but alcohol disrupts sleep in ways melatonin can't fix. See [melatonin and alcohol](/never-hungover/melatonin-and-alcohol).

The general rule: if a supplement is meant to make you calm or sleepy, it will probably add to alcohol's effects, so don't use it as an after-party wind-down.

## Who Should Avoid Mixing CBD and Alcohol

Mixing the two is a bad idea, and using CBD at all deserves a conversation with a doctor first, if you:

- Take prescription medicines, especially those listed above
- Have liver disease or have been told your liver enzymes are high
- Drink heavily or most days
- Are pregnant or breastfeeding (the FDA advises against CBD use during pregnancy and breastfeeding)
- Are an older adult, or prone to falls, since added sedation and unsteadiness raise the risk of injury
- Need to drive, look after children, or be alert afterward

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help

Mixing modest amounts of CBD and alcohol rarely causes an emergency, but large amounts of alcohol plus any sedative can. Get medical help right away (call 911 in the US) if someone:

- Is very hard to wake or can't be woken
- Is breathing slowly, irregularly, or making gurgling sounds
- Is vomiting while drowsy or semi-conscious (roll them onto their side)
- Has blue-tinged or very pale, cold, clammy skin
- Is seriously confused or has a seizure

These are signs of alcohol poisoning or dangerous over-sedation, and they need care, not sleep. If a child or pet gets into CBD or cannabis edibles, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US).

For less urgent concerns, such as feeling unusually drowsy for a long time after mixing, or noticing yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or pain under your right ribs while using CBD regularly, see a doctor soon and mention both your CBD use and your drinking.

## A Better Plan for Your Night Out

If you're thinking about CBD because you want a gentler night or a better morning, here's what actually has the best track record:

- **Choose one, not both.** If you want CBD, make it a CBD night with no alcohol, or swap some drinks for a CBD-only drink rather than mixing.
- **If you're drinking,** eat a real meal first, pace yourself, alternate drinks with water, and stop earlier than you think you need to. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.
- **Buy carefully.** If you use CBD, choose brands that publish a recent third-party lab certificate (often called a COA) showing CBD content and THC levels. Avoid products with health claims that sound too good to be true.
- **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with a small amount of human data, including a 2015 randomized trial in people with fatty liver disease that found improvements in some liver markers. It's promising, not proven, and there is no good evidence that DHM makes it safe to combine CBD and alcohol or changes the advice above. Because DHM may also act on the brain's GABA system, it's simplest not to stack it with CBD and alcohol in the same night. For ordinary drinking nights, popular picks include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.
- **Milk thistle** is the most-studied liver herb, with mixed human evidence but a good safety record. See our [best liver supplements guide](/never-hungover/best-liver-supplements) for how the options compare.

## The Bottom Line

CBD and alcohol aren't a dangerous pair for most healthy adults at modest doses, but they aren't a good team either. Both can make you drowsy and slow, the little human research we have suggests they add to each other, and both lean on your liver. CBD's biggest real-world risks come from interactions with prescription medicines and from products that don't contain what the label says, including hidden THC. There is no good evidence that CBD prevents or treats hangovers or protects your liver from alcohol. If you like CBD, the smartest use is as a swap for a drink, not a mixer with one. And if you take prescription medicines, have liver problems, or drink most days, talk to your doctor before trying it.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is it safe to mix CBD and alcohol?**

For most healthy adults, a modest CBD dose with one or two drinks is unlikely to cause serious harm, but both can cause drowsiness and slow reactions, and they appear to add to each other. Don't drive after mixing them. If you take prescription medicines, have liver disease, or drink most days, talk to your doctor before combining them.

**Does CBD make you more drunk?**

It can make you feel more impaired. In a small human study, people given CBD with alcohol had worse coordination than with placebo, even though their blood alcohol levels were slightly lower. A lower blood alcohol reading doesn't mean you're safer to drive.

**Can CBD help with a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that CBD helps with a hangover. No controlled trial has tested it. Hangovers are driven mostly by poor sleep, dehydration, acetaldehyde, and inflammation, which CBD isn't known to fix. Water, food, rest, and drinking less are what help.

**How long after taking CBD can I drink alcohol?**

There's no official waiting time. The effects of an oil or gummy usually build over one to two hours and fade over several hours, but CBD stays in the body longer, especially with daily use. Wait until you know how a product affects you before adding alcohol, keep both doses small, and don't drive.

**Are CBD drinks a good alternative to alcohol?**

As a replacement, a CBD-only drink from a brand with third-party lab results is a reasonable option for most healthy adults. Many contain little CBD, labels aren't always accurate, and some "hemp drinks" contain THC, so read the label. Mixing CBD drinks with alcohol adds sedation without much benefit.

**Is CBD bad for your liver if you drink?**

At typical retail doses in healthy people, the liver risk is probably low. High-dose CBD can raise liver enzymes on its own, and heavy drinking strains the liver, so the risk rises if you combine large amounts of both or take other medicines processed by the liver. Ask your doctor about a liver test if you use CBD regularly and drink often.

**Does CBD reduce alcohol cravings?**

There is no good evidence yet that CBD reliably helps people drink less. Animal studies and early small human studies are interesting, but CBD isn't an approved treatment for anything alcohol-related. If you get shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you stop drinking, talk to a doctor, because alcohol withdrawal needs proper medical care.

**Can CBD make me fail a drug test?**

Yes, it can. Drug tests look for THC, and full-spectrum CBD products contain small amounts of it, while some products labeled "THC-free" have been found to contain THC. If you're tested, choose a product with a recent lab certificate showing no detectable THC, and know there's still some risk.

**Does DHM make it safe to mix CBD and alcohol?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM protects against the combined sedation of CBD and alcohol or changes how they interact. DHM has promising early research on alcohol metabolism and liver health, mostly from animal studies, but the advice to keep both doses modest, avoid driving, and check with your doctor about medicines still applies.
